transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ellen Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Amira Khan (Skyline Head of ML), Ethan Cole (Skyline Platform), Priya Desai (Skyline Security)

Agenda: 
- Quick intros and context (5m)
- Current infra & pain points (10m)
- Reliability / fallback requirements & SLOs (20m)
- Private/Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs (15m)
- Next steps & recap (5m)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Skyline evaluating Redwood for production LLM inference; main concerns are predictable latency during bursts, graceful degradation strategies (fallback to cheaper models or cached outputs), multi-region failover time, and enterprise audit/SOC2/KMS controls. Customer asked for pricing and config templates to compare dedicated vs hosted.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00] Ellen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Ellen from Redwood, I do AE for the west coast accounts. Quick intros. Marco, you want to say hi?
[00:12] Marco: Yeah hi, Marco Diaz, solutions eng, I mostly focus on infra and routing, hi all.
[00:18] Amira: Amira Khan, Head of ML at Skyline. We're the folks building the customer-facing assistant and some internal workflows.
[00:25] Ethan: Ethan Cole, platform engineer, I own our inference infra and cost ops.
[00:30] Priya: Priya Desai, security lead. I'll be watching the compliance and key management side.

[00:45] Ellen: Great, quick setup: you filled out the qual, thanks — I saw notes about p95 / p50 targets and some on-prem leads. Today we want to focus on reliability and fallout behavior: what happens when a region degraded, how do we failover, what SLOs you expect, and what security constraints push you to Dedicated or Private.

[01:05] Amira: Yes, so high level we serve interactive chat threads — typical p50 requirement is sub-200ms for short prompts, but more importantly p95 needs to be consistent. Our product folks say anything above 700ms p95 impacts NPS. We also have episodic spikes with batch ingestion.

[01:30] Ethan: To add, our current stack is a mix: prototypes on managed SageMaker endpoints, but most prod traffic goes to a k8s cluster with a homegrown batching layer. We're seeing cold-start + kv cache warmup issues on scale-ups.

[01:50] Marco: That's super useful context. When you say kv cache, do you mean a per-pod prefix cache or global cache?
[01:58] Ethan: Right now per-pod, which means when we scale out we get lots of cache misses and latency blips.

[02:10] Marco: Common problem. Redwood has a couple of levers here: we do automatic prefix caching, model variant warm pools, and continuous batching so you don't pay the full cold start penalty during autoscale. For Dedicated we can allocate a warm pool to keep a minimum set of slots live.

[02:30] Amira: Can you explain the "fallback" options? If the primary region is flapping, we need a predictable policy — ideally automatic switchover or returning a degraded but workable result, not an error.

[02:45] Marco: Sure. We typically recommend two-tier fallbacks: soft fallback and hard fallback. Soft fallback is route-level: if p95 breaches we route a subset of traffic to a cheaper model variant or to a cached response. Hard fallback is multi-region failover where requests get routed to another region's pool. We can also do hybrid: try local cheaper model then remote full model.

[03:10] Priya: How fast is a multi-region failover? DNS TTLs and in-flight sessions complicate things, plus we have regulatory constraints on data locality sometimes.

[03:22] Marco: Fair. With our smart routing and health checks, we can detect a regional outage in under 10 seconds and start routing away; end-to-end failover times are usually in the 10–60s window depending on client side TTL and session binding. We also support a sticky session policy and token-based affinity that can be expired quickly to speed cutover.

[03:45] Ethan: 10–60s is a broad range — for some latency sensitive flows we need under 15s failover. Is that realistic?

[03:54] Marco: Under 15s is possible if you configure lower DNS TTLs, use active health probes, and avoid long-lived TCP sticky sessions. Also, Dedicated or Private deployments reduce the network variance; if you're in the same cloud region and using VPC peering it's faster.

[04:15] Amira: If we route to a cheaper model variant during a region blip, how do you preserve semantic fidelity? Some of our flows depend on longer context and those smaller models might hallucinate.

[04:28] Marco: Good point. Fallback variants are configurable per-route. You can specify quality thresholds: e.g., allow fallback only for prompts under X tokens or for non-critical paths. Redwood Optimize can analyze prompt sets and recommend which prompts are safe for downgrade. We also support automatic rollback if quality regressions are detected in the eval harness.

[04:50] Amira: Can Redwood run the eval suite against fallback models to estimate expected degradation?

[04:56] Marco: Yes — we can run your prompt set through both the primary and fallback models and provide an estimated similarity/regression score. That helps quantify tradeoffs.

[05:10] Priya: Switching to security: encryption at rest is required, KMS integration too. We have an HSM-backed KMS for certain keys. Does Redwood Dedicated/Private support external KMS or HSM integration?

[05:23] Ellen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integration. Dedicated (Redwood-managed infra but single-tenant) also supports customer KMS via an integration pattern — we can present options. We'll include the security playbook in the follow-up.

[05:40] Priya: And audit logs — we need token-level tracing for 90 days, stored in a way that meets our compliance team needs.

[05:49] Ellen: We have per-token cost and latency breakdowns and audit logs. Retention windows are configurable; for Private we can match your retention policy, and for Hosted we offer add-on retention windows.

[06:05] Ethan: On SLAs — our legal team expects an SLA that covers regional availability and latency SLOs with credit language. What are typical commitments?

[06:15] Ellen: Our Dedicated contracts often include a 99.9% uptime SLI for model-serving endpoints, with SLOs for p95 latency on selected routes. Hosted is more flexible but not always financially-backed unless you purchase an SLA add-on. We'll send sample SLA wording.

[06:34] Amira: What does "99.9% uptime" mean for a multi-region app? Do you measure region-level or global?

[06:42] Marco: We define the SLI per endpoint and region by default. For global apps you can define a composite SLO (e.g., at least one region available) but a global SLO is often harder to guarantee. We'll share examples of SLO definitions.

[07:00] Ethan: On the ops side, during incidents we want graceful degradation not full fail to 503s. Are there built-in circuit-breakers?

[07:09] Marco: Yes. We support circuit-breakers, backpressure, rate-limiting, and automatic model shedding. You can set thresholds to return cached responses, compressed outputs, or degrade to shorter completions.

[07:24] Amira: How do you handle stateful chat and conversation KV if we move between regions mid-conversation?

[07:33] Marco: For conversation state we recommend either replicated KV with eventual consistency for non-critical metadata, or pin the session to a region and do best-effort sync. If you need strict locality, Private deployment with cross-region replication controlled by you may be better.

[07:50] Priya: We also need a runbook for failures — like what happens if a model process OOMs or there's a GPU driver crash. Do you provide playbooks?

[07:58] Marco: Yes, Redwood provides operational playbooks: detection, automatic restart, draining, and warming of replacement workers. For Dedicated we'll run canary deployments and offer a rollback policy. We also integrate with common alerting stacks (PagerDuty, Opsgenie).

[08:15] Amira: There's the cost question — if we keep warm pools for low latency that's expensive. Any knobs to reduce cost while preserving p95?

[08:24] Marco: A few: intelligent batching with lower latency targets, prefix KV caching to avoid recomputing prefixes, quantized model variants for cheaper inference on non-critical paths, and autoscale policies tuned for their tail distribution. Dedicated gives better price predictability; Hosted can be cheaper if you accept more fallbacks.

[08:45] Ethan: Does Redwood provide tooling to simulate burst patterns to validate autoscale and fallback configs?

[08:52] Marco: Yep, we can replay anonymized traffic and run synthetic load tests. If you share a 72-hour sample I can run a replay and show how different configs behave.

[09:05] Amira: Ok, timeline: we want to decide vendor by end of Q4, pilot in Q1, rollout in Q2.

[09:14] Ellen: Makes sense. We'll aim to get pricing and technical templates out this week. Marco will craft two fallback topologies: one for multi-region active-passive, another for single-region degraded-mode.

[09:28] Priya: A couple of nitty-gritty questions — data residency: if we failover to another region, is data persisted there? We have contractual obligations in some markets.

[09:36] Marco: Failover can be configured to either route and process data remotely or to stop processing certain regulated endpoints. You can add route-level residency constraints so we won't automatically route sensitive data to another region.

[09:50] Amira: What about session affinity and TTL — our clients sometimes use long-lived websockets and ephemeral keys.

[09:58] Marco: Websockets complicate failover but we offer keepalive and graceful session migration strategies. For ephemeral keys, you can reduce token TTLs so that during an outage clients reauthenticate to a healthy region quickly.

[10:15] Ethan: Competitor checks — we've looked at SageMaker multi-AZ endpoints and OpenAI for baseline. What does Redwood bring that they don't?

[10:25] Ellen: Two things: inference-first operational controls (fine-grained routing, prefix caching, rollout controls) and unified experience across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Plus we focus on predictable unit cost and observability at the token level.

[10:40] Amira: Security more — about SSO and SCIM — we use SAML SSO and need RBAC synched with SCIM. Is that supported?

[10:48] Ellen: Yes, SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM for user provisioning are supported for Dedicated and Private; Hosted supports SSO and API token management. We'll include the integration guide.

[11:05] Ethan: A weird edge-case: if DNS fails for a region, can clients be prepopulated with prioritized endpoint lists?

[11:13] Marco: You can configure client libraries with multiple endpoints and a priority order, and Redwood SDK supports failover heuristics. That reduces reliance on DNS.

[11:25] Priya: Auditing again — we need immutable logs for a year for some customers, and redaction options for PII.

[11:33] Ellen: For Private we can handle immutability and redaction via your storage; Hosted supports configurable retention and optional PII redaction filters. We'll send the security doc with retention and redaction options.

[11:50] Amira: Let's talk about incident simulations — do you do runbook dry-runs?

[11:57] Marco: We run table-top exercises with customers and can run a controlled failover to a staging region. We recommend a chaos-style test to validate stats and rerouting.

[12:12] Ethan: Great. If we pilot, will Redwood give a small reserved Dedicated slice for realistic testing?

[12:20] Ellen: We often do pilot credits and temporary reserved capacity for pilots to emulate production. We'll propose a pilot configuration in the follow-up.

[12:35] Amira: Regarding monitoring, is tracing per-request available? We need token-level traces for debugging bad outputs.

[12:43] Marco: Yes, distributed tracing hooks available — we can include sample instrumentation. Token-level traces are available, but you can redact or limit them for privacy.

[13:00] Ethan: Can Redwood's routing do weighted routing across regions for traffic shaping?

[13:07] Marco: Yep. Weighted routing, canary percentages, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback thresholds are all supported.

[13:22] Priya: Any limitations on private deployments regarding hardware? We have some on-prem GPUs we want to use.

[13:30] Ellen: Private supports customer-owned hardware in on-prem packages; we'll need to do an infra assessment. For HSM/KMS integration there's a bit more ops work but it's supported.

[13:45] Amira: About model versioning during failover — if we fail to another region that is slightly behind on model rollout, how do you ensure consistency?

[13:55] Marco: Model pinning and rollout windows are key. You can pin a region to a specific model version and only allow failover to regions with compatible versions; we also support gradual rollout to keep parity.

[14:10] Ethan: Any telemetry we can export into our internal dashboards?

[14:15] Ellen: Yes, you can stream metrics to Prometheus, send traces to your APM, and export logs to your storage via S3 or GCS.

[14:28] Amira: Ok let's get practical — can you sketch two fallback topologies and the tradeoffs?

[14:36] Marco: Sure. Topology A: Multi-region active-passive, warm standbys in secondary region, automatic routing to secondary on failure, higher cost but sub-30s failover. Topology B: Single-region with local fallbacks (cheaper model + cache), much lower cost but some degradation in output quality and no cross-region resilience. I'll put config details in the templates.

[14:58] Amira: For topology A what's the expected extra cost? ballpark.

[15:04] Marco: Usually 25–50% extra depending on warm pool size; depends on concurrency and warm-worker count. Dedicated reserved capacity reduces that premium.

[15:20] Ethan: When you say warm-workers, are those fully allocated GPUs or lightweight warmed containers?

[15:27] Marco: They're reserved slots on GPU hosts with preloaded weights — you can choose smaller quantized variants for less memory if acceptable.

[15:40] Priya: If we require that all PII never leaves region, that affects the multi-region plan.

[15:47] Marco: Correct, we'd scope sensitive routes to region-only processing and only failover non-sensitive traffic. Route-level residency constraints handle that.

[16:00] Amira: On rollback — if a fallback model introduces regressions, how fast can you flip back?

[16:08] Marco: Instant rollback is possible; we also provide automatic regression detection tied to your eval prompts and can trigger rollbacks when deviation passes thresholds.

[16:20] Ellen: Quick note — we'll attach our reliability playbook and an example SLO matrix.

[16:28] Amira: Anything about data plane encryption in flight? TLS mutual auth?

[16:33] Priya: We use mTLS for internal services.

[16:36] Marco: We support mTLS and mutual-auth for Private and Dedicated setups; Hosted uses TLS with optional client certs for dedicated enterprise accounts.

[16:50] Ethan: For the pilot, can we test failover under realistic traffic?

[16:55] Marco: Yes, with a replay of your 72h sample. I'll include instructions and will run replay internally against the templates.

[17:10] Amira: One more question on observability — can Redwood surface prompt-level QoR metrics? like hallucination rates?

[17:18] Marco: We can calculate regression/similarity metrics versus reference outputs; hallucination detection is possible but is heuristic-based — Redwood Optimize can help craft benchmarks.

[17:32] Ellen: Ok wrapping up, sounds like main blockers are security signoff, cost comparison, and pilot configuration. We'll get the docs and templates out.

[17:45] Priya: Please include specifics on KMS/HSM integration steps and what is required from our infra team.

[17:52] Ellen: Noted.

[18:00] Amira: Also include sample SLO wording for p95 and p50, and how credits are calculated.

[18:06] Ellen: Will do.

[18:12] Ethan: We'll aim to get the traffic sample by next Friday.

[18:17] Ellen: Great. Any other questions?

[18:22] Amira: No, thanks. Looks good.

[18:26] Ellen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the price/SLO matrix and the two fallback templates.

End of meeting.
